title: Ad Creative Ultra-Premium Cinematic System for Crypto Wallet | reduce bounce 40% | PID 00001
prompt_content:
EXECUTION BRIEF — AD CREATIVE

ROLE
Act as a senior commercial video director, motion designer, editor, and prompt engineer. Your job is to produce an executable shot plan and generation brief, not a generic “premium cinematic” description. Optimize for a believable finished video that an editor can assemble and a video model can reproduce consistently.

PROJECT
Industry: Crypto Wallet
Audience: a crypto user who values simple control, clear confirmation, and security cues over hype
Primary problem: wallet actions can feel risky or confusing when confirmation and asset status are unclear
Creative goal: reduce bounce 40%
Goal interpretation: clarity and immediate relevance
Business objective: Make the first visual answer the visitor's likely question: “Is this for me, and what does it do?” Do not interpret the goal as permission to add louder effects or unrelated hooks.
Category: Ad Creative
Target duration: 10–15 seconds
Format: 16:9 master plus a 9:16 crop-safe composition when requested

CREATIVE CONCEPT
Center the video on one wallet action such as receive, send, or review a transaction. The viewer should understand the situation before the first third of the runtime. make the sequence legible: intent → confirmation → completed state, with supplied UI for exact values

The creative should feel clean real environment, using soft window daylight. Use a 50mm visual language and slow slider push-in. Keep the camera movement subordinate to the message: motion should reveal, compare, demonstrate, or create emphasis—not exist merely to look expensive.

CATEGORY EXECUTION
0–2s pattern interrupt; 2–6s problem and product action; 6–10s proof/benefit; final 2–3s clean CTA or brand hold.
Build one visual idea, not a montage of unrelated benefits. The opening frame must communicate the subject without relying on tiny text.
Keep continuity locked across shots: same subject identity, wardrobe/materials, environment, light direction, and product geometry.

SHOT-BY-SHOT PLAN
1. OPENING — Establish the subject and problem immediately. Specify the starting frame, subject position, action, and what changes during the first 1–2 seconds. No logo-only opening.
2. DEVELOPMENT — Show the single core action. Give each shot one job. If the story needs multiple steps, cut only when the information changes.
3. PROOF — Show an observable product behavior, physical detail, customer moment, or supplied evidence that supports the claim. Never substitute abstract “success” imagery for actual proof.
4. PAYOFF — Resolve the action with a clear end state. Leave enough clean screen time for approved copy or CTA when the format requires it.
5. END/LOOP — For looping formats, design the last movement to return naturally to the opening state. For non-looping formats, end on the strongest useful frame rather than a decorative logo animation.

CONTINUITY RULES
Keep the main subject consistent in shape, color, material, identity, wardrobe, hand position, and environment. Keep lighting direction and focal length stable unless a deliberate shot change is specified. Do not morph between unrelated objects. Do not change the product design from shot to shot.
For exact interface or packaging text, use supplied assets and add typography in post. Do not ask the generation model to invent legible small text.

AUDIO / EDIT
Use a restrained music bed and 1–2 purposeful SFX; keep the CTA intelligible.
Edit on action or information change. Avoid excessive whip pans, speed ramps, glitch transitions, or artificial “epic” impacts. Preserve enough natural pauses for comprehension. Captions, legal lines, product claims, and CTA copy should be added from approved text during post-production.

CLAIM AND ASSET DISCIPLINE
Do not imply guaranteed returns, guaranteed security, price appreciation, or fabricate balances/transaction IDs.
Only use product facts, customer quotes, statistics, certifications, medical/financial claims, property details, or performance claims that are supplied and approved. If a required fact is missing, mark it as [APPROVED INPUT REQUIRED] rather than inventing it.

NEGATIVE / FAILURE CONDITIONS
No flicker, temporal instability, object morphing, identity drift, warped hands, duplicate objects, impossible reflections, fake UI text, accidental logos, watermarks, unreadable captions, random camera shake, excessive motion blur, plastic skin, generic stock-footage look, or visual elements unrelated to the core problem. Do not add a second product, second narrative, or second CTA.

OUTPUT SPECIFICATION
Return:
• a concise concept statement;
• the ordered shot list with approximate seconds, framing, camera action, subject action, environment, lighting, and transition;
• the exact generation prompt for each shot;
• the negative prompt shared by the shots;
• post-production notes for supplied UI, captions, CTA, color, sound, and export;
• one fallback shot for any scene that is likely to fail in generation.

QUALITY GATE
The first 2 seconds must contain visible subject/action; the benefit must be understandable from picture and supplied copy; CTA must have clean screen time.
Also verify:
- The first frame makes the subject and context identifiable.
- Every shot has one clear purpose.
- The core product/subject remains consistent.
- No unsupported claims are introduced.
- The requested aspect ratio and duration are achievable without relying on invisible or contradictory instructions.
- The result could be handed directly to a director/editor without asking what “premium” means.
- The creative goal is treated as an optimization target, not a guaranteed outcome.

SUCCESS TEST
A professional reviewer should be able to answer “Who is this for?”, “What is happening?”, “Why should I care?”, and “What should I do next?” from the finished cut. Make the first visual answer the visitor's likely question: “Is this for me, and what does it do?” Do not interpret the goal as permission to add louder effects or unrelated hooks.

EXECUTION BRIEF — WEBSITE HERO VIDEO

ROLE
Act as a senior commercial video director, motion designer, editor, and prompt engineer. Your job is to produce an executable shot plan and generation brief, not a generic “premium cinematic” description. Optimize for a believable finished video that an editor can assemble and a video model can reproduce consistently.

PROJECT
Industry: DTC Skincare
Audience: a skincare shopper comparing products and looking for credible texture and routine cues
Primary problem: uncertainty about texture, application, and whether the product fits a simple routine
Creative goal: re-engage 10k users
Goal interpretation: freshness without confusion
Business objective: Use a recognizable product cue with one new angle or behavior. The creative should reward returning viewers without assuming they remember previous campaigns.
Category: Website Hero Video
Target duration: 6–10 seconds, seamless loop
Format: 16:9, silent by default, responsive crop-safe composition

CREATIVE CONCEPT
Center the video on the actual skincare package, cream/serum texture, and a believable application moment. The viewer should understand the situation before the first third of the runtime. show texture, amount, spread, finish, and packaging details that can be verified from supplied assets

The creative should feel architectural interior, using controlled studio softbox. Use a 50mm visual language and locked-off frame with subject movement. Keep the camera movement subordinate to the message: motion should reveal, compare, demonstrate, or create emphasis—not exist merely to look expensive.

CATEGORY EXECUTION
single continuous action with a visually clean beginning/end match.
Design for muted autoplay and fast loading. Keep the focal subject away from likely navigation/CTA overlays and avoid tiny details that disappear on mobile.
Build a true visual loop: match subject position, light direction, and camera phase at the seam. Export a lightweight web version separately from the high-quality master.

SHOT-BY-SHOT PLAN
1. OPENING — Establish the subject and problem immediately. Specify the starting frame, subject position, action, and what changes during the first 1–2 seconds. No logo-only opening.
2. DEVELOPMENT — Show the single core action. Give each shot one job. If the story needs multiple steps, cut only when the information changes.
3. PROOF — Show an observable product behavior, physical detail, customer moment, or supplied evidence that supports the claim. Never substitute abstract “success” imagery for actual proof.
4. PAYOFF — Resolve the action with a clear end state. Leave enough clean screen time for approved copy or CTA when the format requires it.
5. END/LOOP — For looping formats, design the last movement to return naturally to the opening state. For non-looping formats, end on the strongest useful frame rather than a decorative logo animation.

CONTINUITY RULES
Keep the main subject consistent in shape, color, material, identity, wardrobe, hand position, and environment. Keep lighting direction and focal length stable unless a deliberate shot change is specified. Do not morph between unrelated objects. Do not change the product design from shot to shot.
For exact interface or packaging text, use supplied assets and add typography in post. Do not ask the generation model to invent legible small text.

AUDIO / EDIT
None in the default hero asset.
Edit on action or information change. Avoid excessive whip pans, speed ramps, glitch transitions, or artificial “epic” impacts. Preserve enough natural pauses for comprehension. Captions, legal lines, product claims, and CTA copy should be added from approved text during post-production.

CLAIM AND ASSET DISCIPLINE
Do not promise medical outcomes, invent ingredients, or create unnaturally perfect skin.
Only use product facts, customer quotes, statistics, certifications, medical/financial claims, property details, or performance claims that are supplied and approved. If a required fact is missing, mark it as [APPROVED INPUT REQUIRED] rather than inventing it.

NEGATIVE / FAILURE CONDITIONS
No flicker, temporal instability, object morphing, identity drift, warped hands, duplicate objects, impossible reflections, fake UI text, accidental logos, watermarks, unreadable captions, random camera shake, excessive motion blur, plastic skin, generic stock-footage look, or visual elements unrelated to the core problem. Do not add a second product, second narrative, or second CTA.

OUTPUT SPECIFICATION
Return:
• a concise concept statement;
• the ordered shot list with approximate seconds, framing, camera action, subject action, environment, lighting, and transition;
• the exact generation prompt for each shot;
• the negative prompt shared by the shots;
• post-production notes for supplied UI, captions, CTA, color, sound, and export;
• one fallback shot for any scene that is likely to fail in generation.

QUALITY GATE
The loop must not reveal a hard cut; the first frame must already look intentional; no essential information may depend on text or sound.
Also verify:
- The first frame makes the subject and context identifiable.
- Every shot has one clear purpose.
- The core product/subject remains consistent.
- No unsupported claims are introduced.
- The requested aspect ratio and duration are achievable without relying on invisible or contradictory instructions.
- The result could be handed directly to a director/editor without asking what “premium” means.
- The creative goal is treated as an optimization target, not a guaranteed outcome.

SUCCESS TEST
A professional reviewer should be able to answer “Who is this for?”, “What is happening?”, “Why should I care?”, and “What should I do next?” from the finished cut. Use a recognizable product cue with one new angle or behavior. The creative should reward returning viewers without assuming they remember previous campaigns.

EXECUTION BRIEF — WEBSITE HERO VIDEO

ROLE
Act as a senior commercial video director, motion designer, editor, and prompt engineer. Your job is to produce an executable shot plan and generation brief, not a generic “premium cinematic” description. Optimize for a believable finished video that an editor can assemble and a video model can reproduce consistently.

PROJECT
Industry: Luxury Real Estate
Audience: a high-intent buyer evaluating whether a property feels distinctive enough to justify a viewing
Primary problem: listing media often shows rooms but fails to communicate flow, light, materials, and lived experience
Creative goal: launch product 30 days
Goal interpretation: launch readiness
Business objective: Prioritize a repeatable asset that can be approved, captioned, cropped, and published quickly. Avoid production techniques that require fragile continuity or heavy VFX.
Category: Website Hero Video
Target duration: 6–10 seconds, seamless loop
Format: 16:9, silent by default, responsive crop-safe composition

CREATIVE CONCEPT
Center the video on one property and one coherent route through it, anchored by a signature space. The viewer should understand the situation before the first third of the runtime. show real architectural details: arrival, transition, hero room, material close-up, view

The creative should feel natural kitchen/vanity, using overcast natural light. Use a 65mm macro visual language and slow slider push-in. Keep the camera movement subordinate to the message: motion should reveal, compare, demonstrate, or create emphasis—not exist merely to look expensive.

CATEGORY EXECUTION
single continuous action with a visually clean beginning/end match.
Design for muted autoplay and fast loading. Keep the focal subject away from likely navigation/CTA overlays and avoid tiny details that disappear on mobile.
Build a true visual loop: match subject position, light direction, and camera phase at the seam. Export a lightweight web version separately from the high-quality master.

SHOT-BY-SHOT PLAN
1. OPENING — Establish the subject and problem immediately. Specify the starting frame, subject position, action, and what changes during the first 1–2 seconds. No logo-only opening.
2. DEVELOPMENT — Show the single core action. Give each shot one job. If the story needs multiple steps, cut only when the information changes.
3. PROOF — Show an observable product behavior, physical detail, customer moment, or supplied evidence that supports the claim. Never substitute abstract “success” imagery for actual proof.
4. PAYOFF — Resolve the action with a clear end state. Leave enough clean screen time for approved copy or CTA when the format requires it.
5. END/LOOP — For looping formats, design the last movement to return naturally to the opening state. For non-looping formats, end on the strongest useful frame rather than a decorative logo animation.

CONTINUITY RULES
Keep the main subject consistent in shape, color, material, identity, wardrobe, hand position, and environment. Keep lighting direction and focal length stable unless a deliberate shot change is specified. Do not morph between unrelated objects. Do not change the product design from shot to shot.
For exact interface or packaging text, use supplied assets and add typography in post. Do not ask the generation model to invent legible small text.

AUDIO / EDIT
None in the default hero asset.
Edit on action or information change. Avoid excessive whip pans, speed ramps, glitch transitions, or artificial “epic” impacts. Preserve enough natural pauses for comprehension. Captions, legal lines, product claims, and CTA copy should be added from approved text during post-production.

CLAIM AND ASSET DISCIPLINE
Do not invent rooms, views, amenities, square footage, finishes, or neighborhood claims not present in supplied assets.
Only use product facts, customer quotes, statistics, certifications, medical/financial claims, property details, or performance claims that are supplied and approved. If a required fact is missing, mark it as [APPROVED INPUT REQUIRED] rather than inventing it.

NEGATIVE / FAILURE CONDITIONS
No flicker, temporal instability, object morphing, identity drift, warped hands, duplicate objects, impossible reflections, fake UI text, accidental logos, watermarks, unreadable captions, random camera shake, excessive motion blur, plastic skin, generic stock-footage look, or visual elements unrelated to the core problem. Do not add a second product, second narrative, or second CTA.

OUTPUT SPECIFICATION
Return:
• a concise concept statement;
• the ordered shot list with approximate seconds, framing, camera action, subject action, environment, lighting, and transition;
• the exact generation prompt for each shot;
• the negative prompt shared by the shots;
• post-production notes for supplied UI, captions, CTA, color, sound, and export;
• one fallback shot for any scene that is likely to fail in generation.

QUALITY GATE
The loop must not reveal a hard cut; the first frame must already look intentional; no essential information may depend on text or sound.
Also verify:
- The first frame makes the subject and context identifiable.
- Every shot has one clear purpose.
- The core product/subject remains consistent.
- No unsupported claims are introduced.
- The requested aspect ratio and duration are achievable without relying on invisible or contradictory instructions.
- The result could be handed directly to a director/editor without asking what “premium” means.
- The creative goal is treated as an optimization target, not a guaranteed outcome.

SUCCESS TEST
A professional reviewer should be able to answer “Who is this for?”, “What is happening?”, “Why should I care?”, and “What should I do next?” from the finished cut. Prioritize a repeatable asset that can be approved, captioned, cropped, and published quickly. Avoid production techniques that require fragile continuity or heavy VFX.

EXECUTION BRIEF — TUTORIAL

ROLE
Act as a senior commercial video director, motion designer, editor, and prompt engineer. Your job is to produce an executable shot plan and generation brief, not a generic “premium cinematic” description. Optimize for a believable finished video that an editor can assemble and a video model can reproduce consistently.

PROJECT
Industry: Luxury Real Estate
Audience: a high-intent buyer evaluating whether a property feels distinctive enough to justify a viewing
Primary problem: listing media often shows rooms but fails to communicate flow, light, materials, and lived experience
Creative goal: increase watch time 32%
Goal interpretation: progressive reveal
Business objective: Hold attention by revealing useful information in stages. Avoid arbitrary speed ramps, constant camera motion, or delayed relevance.
Category: Tutorial
Target duration: 45–75 seconds, designed as modular 8–15 second scenes
Format: 16:9 primary; keep center-safe composition for later crops

CREATIVE CONCEPT
Center the video on one property and one coherent route through it, anchored by a signature space. The viewer should understand the situation before the first third of the runtime. show real architectural details: arrival, transition, hero room, material close-up, view

The creative should feel minimal office desk, using large diffused key with subtle rim. Use a 65mm macro visual language and slow slider push-in. Keep the camera movement subordinate to the message: motion should reveal, compare, demonstrate, or create emphasis—not exist merely to look expensive.

CATEGORY EXECUTION
Hook the task; establish starting state; perform 3–5 numbered actions; show completed state; end with one verification cue.
Treat each step as its own shot. Maintain the same person, device, environment, wardrobe, and interface state across adjacent shots.
Keep continuity locked across shots: same subject identity, wardrobe/materials, environment, light direction, and product geometry.

SHOT-BY-SHOT PLAN
1. OPENING — Establish the subject and problem immediately. Specify the starting frame, subject position, action, and what changes during the first 1–2 seconds. No logo-only opening.
2. DEVELOPMENT — Show the single core action. Give each shot one job. If the story needs multiple steps, cut only when the information changes.
3. PROOF — Show an observable product behavior, physical detail, customer moment, or supplied evidence that supports the claim. Never substitute abstract “success” imagery for actual proof.
4. PAYOFF — Resolve the action with a clear end state. Leave enough clean screen time for approved copy or CTA when the format requires it.
5. END/LOOP — For looping formats, design the last movement to return naturally to the opening state. For non-looping formats, end on the strongest useful frame rather than a decorative logo animation.

CONTINUITY RULES
Keep the main subject consistent in shape, color, material, identity, wardrobe, hand position, and environment. Keep lighting direction and focal length stable unless a deliberate shot change is specified. Do not morph between unrelated objects. Do not change the product design from shot to shot.
For exact interface or packaging text, use supplied assets and add typography in post. Do not ask the generation model to invent legible small text.

AUDIO / EDIT
Clear voiceover or on-screen step labels; use quiet transitions rather than constant music.
Edit on action or information change. Avoid excessive whip pans, speed ramps, glitch transitions, or artificial “epic” impacts. Preserve enough natural pauses for comprehension. Captions, legal lines, product claims, and CTA copy should be added from approved text during post-production.

CLAIM AND ASSET DISCIPLINE
Do not invent rooms, views, amenities, square footage, finishes, or neighborhood claims not present in supplied assets.
Only use product facts, customer quotes, statistics, certifications, medical/financial claims, property details, or performance claims that are supplied and approved. If a required fact is missing, mark it as [APPROVED INPUT REQUIRED] rather than inventing it.

NEGATIVE / FAILURE CONDITIONS
No flicker, temporal instability, object morphing, identity drift, warped hands, duplicate objects, impossible reflections, fake UI text, accidental logos, watermarks, unreadable captions, random camera shake, excessive motion blur, plastic skin, generic stock-footage look, or visual elements unrelated to the core problem. Do not add a second product, second narrative, or second CTA.

OUTPUT SPECIFICATION
Return:
• a concise concept statement;
• the ordered shot list with approximate seconds, framing, camera action, subject action, environment, lighting, and transition;
• the exact generation prompt for each shot;
• the negative prompt shared by the shots;
• post-production notes for supplied UI, captions, CTA, color, sound, and export;
• one fallback shot for any scene that is likely to fail in generation.

QUALITY GATE
A viewer should be able to name the task, follow the steps in order, and identify the final successful state without guessing.
Also verify:
- The first frame makes the subject and context identifiable.
- Every shot has one clear purpose.
- The core product/subject remains consistent.
- No unsupported claims are introduced.
- The requested aspect ratio and duration are achievable without relying on invisible or contradictory instructions.
- The result could be handed directly to a director/editor without asking what “premium” means.
- The creative goal is treated as an optimization target, not a guaranteed outcome.

SUCCESS TEST
A professional reviewer should be able to answer “Who is this for?”, “What is happening?”, “Why should I care?”, and “What should I do next?” from the finished cut. Hold attention by revealing useful information in stages. Avoid arbitrary speed ramps, constant camera motion, or delayed relevance.
